% Abstract page
\begin{abstract}
This paper examines the beta anomaly, where stocks with higher betas tend to produce lower risk-adjusted returns than those with lower betas, contradicting a fundamental prediction of the CAPM. This is done by testing Propositions 1 and 2 from Frazzini and Pedersen (2014).
Using US equity data from 1963 to 2025, we test proposition 1 by examining the relationship between beta and alpha to test for the presence of the beta anomaly. To test proposition 2, we construct a BAB portfolio to examine the performance of a strategy which exploits this anomaly by going long on low-beta stocks and short on high-beta stocks.
We find evidence of a negative relationship between beta and alpha, which supports proposition 1 and confirms that the beta anomaly is present, leading to a flatter security market line. We also find that the BAB portfolio generates positive risk-adjusted returns, which supports proposition 2. However, when we introduce transaction costs, the estimated cost drag overwhelms the gross return under the assumption of full monthly rebalancing, though this represents an upper bound on true implementation costs.
\end{abstract}
